written.myAnswer: During G1, the cell grows, carries out normal metabolic activities, synthesizes RNA and proteins, and increases its organelles.
DNA is replicated, so each chromosome consists of two sister chromatids.
Crossing over exchanges DNA segments between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, creating new combinations of alleles.
Animal cells divide by a cleavage furrow that pinches the cell in two. Plant cells form a cell plate between the daughter nuclei, which develops into a new cell wall.

In mitotic prophase, chromosomes condense, but homologous chromosomes do not pair and crossing over does not occur. In prophase I of meiosis, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over occurs between non-sister chromatids.
Mitosis maintains the chromosome number in daughter cells, whereas meiosis halves it.

Prophase: chromosomes condense and the spindle forms. Metaphase: chromosomes line up at the equator. Anaphase: sister chromatids separate and move to opposite poles. Telophase: nuclear membranes reform around the two chromosome sets.
In animal cells, a cleavage furrow pinches the cytoplasm into two. In plant cells, a cell plate forms between the daughter nuclei, grows outward, and develops into a new cell wall.
Mitosis enables growth, repair, replacement, regeneration, and asexual reproduction in some organisms. It maintains chromosome number and produces genetically identical daughter cells.

In prophase I, homologous chromosomes pair and crossing over occurs. In metaphase I, homologous pairs line up at the equator. In anaphase I, homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids remain together. In telophase I, nuclei may reform, and cytokinesis produces two haploid cells with duplicated chromosomes.
Meiosis produces haploid gametes, helps maintain the species’ chromosome number across generations after fertilization, and creates genetic variation through crossing over and independent assortment.
If checkpoints fail to stop or repair cells with damaged DNA, those cells may continue dividing. Mutations can accumulate, leading to uncontrolled cell division and cancer.

Skin cells divide to replace cells that are continually lost or damaged. Mature nerve and muscle cells are highly specialized and usually remain in a non-dividing state while performing their functions.
